title: Sardines: protein, omega-3, calcium, and calories

seo.title: Sardine nutrition: protein, omega-3, calcium, calories
seo.meta_description: Canned sardines can provide 24–25 g protein, more than 1 g EPA+DHA and several hundred mg calcium per 100 g when the softened bones are eaten.
seo.search_intent: Understand sardine nutrition and why canned bone-in sardines stand out for protein, omega-3 and calcium.

excerpt: Sardines combine three nutrients that are rarely this concentrated in one food: roughly 24–25 grams protein, more than 1 gram EPA+DHA, and—when canned with edible bones—around 300–400 milligrams calcium per 100 grams.
content_html:
Sardines are small fish with an unusually concentrated nutrition profile. A drained can with edible bones combines substantial protein, EPA and DHA, and far more calcium than a boneless fish fillet.

Approximate canned sardine nutrition per 100 g

NutrientTypical drained value
Calories~185–210
Protein~24–25 g
Fat~10–12 g
EPA+DHA~1.3–1.5 g
Calcium, with bones~300–400 mg

Packing medium matters: oil, tomato sauce, water, or other sauces change the final label, and draining changes how much liquid is included in the measured portion.

A small can already provides substantial protein

An 85 g drained serving at 24.5 g protein/100 g provides about 20.8 g protein. That is comparable to many larger servings of other meat or fish foods.

The omega-3 is direct EPA and DHA

NIH lists about 1.19 g EPA+DHA in 3 oz of canned sardines in tomato sauce, drained. That converts to roughly 1.40 g per 100 g.

This is far more than lean hake, which contains only tenths of a gram, although below some Atlantic salmon references above 2 g/100 g.

Why sardines are so high in calcium

The answer is the bones. Canning heat softens the small skeleton enough to eat. Consuming those bones means consuming their mineral content, allowing bone-in entries to reach roughly 300–400 mg calcium/100 g.

If the bones are removed, much of that calcium advantage disappears. Sardine flesh alone is not responsible for several hundred milligrams.

Sardines also supply B12, vitamin D, and selenium

Oily fish are natural B12 foods, and sardines can also provide vitamin D and selenium. Exact amounts vary with species and product, but micronutrient density is substantial.

Sodium depends on the can

Fresh sardines contain natural sodium, while canned products often include added salt. Several hundred milligrams sodium per 100 g is common. Comparing labels is the best way to find a lower-sodium option when that matters.

Does oil-packed mean much higher calories?

Sardines already contain their own fat. Oil-packed versions can be higher in calories if additional packing oil remains with the fish. Ten extra grams of oil equals about 90 calories; draining removes free oil but may not remove all oil retained by the fish.

The useful takeaway

Bone-in canned sardines are a highly concentrated source of protein, EPA+DHA, and calcium. Read the drained weight, packing medium, and sodium. Their remarkable calcium content depends on the softened bones being part of the edible portion.

faq.question: How much protein is in sardines?
faq.answer: Drained canned sardines commonly provide about 24–25 g/100 g; an 85 g serving is roughly 21 g protein.

faq.question: How much omega-3 do sardines have?
faq.answer: NIH lists about 1.19 g EPA+DHA in 3 oz canned sardines in tomato sauce, equivalent to roughly 1.4 g/100 g.

faq.question: Why are sardines high in calcium?
faq.answer: Because the softened bones are edible and contribute much of the calcium.
